transcript:
[00:00] Samira: ok everyone thanks for joining, um we'll try to keep this to 45, 50 mins. quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya: Maya here, hi.
[00:10] Ravi: Ravi on infra.
[00:12] Elena: Elena product.
[00:14] Noah: Noah SRE.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from security.
[00:18] Diego: Diego Redwood SE. Jordan: Jordan CSM.
[00:22] Samira: cool, so agenda — quick readout from last run, dig into autoscale params, decide on Dedicated sizing options and next run. Diego you're up for the run readout.
[00:33] Diego: yep, so the short story — we did a 30 minute sim with three micro-peaks, each peak ~4 minutes, ramp to ~3x baseline qps. overall tail latency at 95th was about 220-280ms for the large model (redwood-bert-1q) when KV cache miss rate spiked. cache hit percentage averaged 62% but dropped to ~28% during the peaks — looks like warmup timing is the culprit.
[01:02] Maya: quick q — that 3x peak is representative, we sometimes see 4–5x at midday but yeah 3x is a conservative baseline.
[01:09] Diego: noted. cpu/gpu util — GPUs hit 85–92% for sustained 80s seconds during peaks, and we saw memory pressure on the H100 nodes, swap didn't happen but there were scheduling retries.
[01:23] Noah: scheduling retries? do you mean preemption or kube pod backoff?
[01:26] Diego: pod backoff, some container restart loops because of config mismatch in local batching window; that's on us — we missed a backpressure setting.
[01:33] Samira: ok can you summarize the failure modes? specifically what would cause user‑facing errors in a production P99 sense.
[01:41] Diego: mostly cold cache + scale up lag. scale-up latency is about 45–60s to get extra workers online when autoscale triggers on cpu/gpu util threshold of 70%. with aggressive ramps, that gap shows up as elevated p99 (1.2–1.8s) for a few seconds. A fallback to a quantized variant reduced p99 to ~420ms but quality drop was notable for some prompts.
[02:07] Ravi: does Redwood have a burst buffer or burst capacity option?
[02:10] Jordan: yes, we have a burst buffer add-on concept — essentially reserved spare warm workers that can be used for short peaks without full scale up. we can configure burst buffer as percent of pool or fixed units.
[02:20] Priya: from security perspective we need the burst nodes to be inside our VPC and use our KMS for model keys — is that supported?
[02:29] Diego: supported — private mode supports customer KMS and VPC peering. small gotcha: if you're using dedicated but with shared control plane there's an extra audit log export step; we'll include details.
[02:40] Elena: on the Dedicated sizing, Samira suggested 8 vs 16 GPU pool models — what's the cost delta and perf tradeoff?
[02:47] Samira: i'll share the spreadsheet after but ballpark, a 16 GPU pool with autoscale gives better absorbtion of a sustained 3–4x ramp without resorting to model fallbacks; but it's roughly 1.7–1.9x the monthly committed cost of an 8 GPU pool. burst buffer reduces the need for immediate scale up but costs extra as a reserved hot buffer.
[03:07] Maya: what's the recommended autoscale policy? we saw 70% util threshold caused lag, is higher better?
[03:12] Diego: recommendation from the run: set scale-up threshold to 60% with a short cool-down of 30s and scale-up granularity of +25% of capacity. scale-down should be more conservative — 10 minute cool-down — to avoid flapping. also increase prefix/KV cache retention so cold misses drop during repeated peaks.
[03:32] Noah: question: if we set a lower threshold we risk over-scaling regular traffic and increasing cost — can we tie policy to traffic shaping by route?
[03:40] Diego: yes, Redwood Console supports per-route policies. you can route high‑priority APIs (like realtime chat) to a faster autoscale profile and cheaper routes to a different pool.
[03:50] Elena: can we do weighted routing to use cheaper quantized models for low-priority requests?
[03:54] Diego: yep, route-by-policy + fallback rules. important to test quality regressions in our eval harness.
[04:00] Samira: ok let's talk about next benchmarking run — we propose a 2 hour sim with three 5-minute peaks at 4x baseline and an injected cold-cache spike mid-run. goals: validate 60% threshold + 30s cool-down + 25% scale increments, compare 8 vs 16 pool costs and run with 40% burst buffer on top.
[04:20] Maya: yes please run that, and also include a run where the fallback quantized model is disabled, we need to see real user impact.
[04:27] Diego: yep we'll do both runs. we'll capture latency percentiles, queue depth histograms and KV cache TTL stats.
[04:32] Priya: for compliance, please also produce an audit log snippet showing node creation/destruction events and KMS key usage — mask PII.
[04:41] Jordan: will do. Samira, do you want to walk through the pricing options now or later?
[04:45] Samira: let's do a quick sketch now. for committed Dedicated — 8 GPU pool is baseline. add burst buffer at 30–40% increases committed cost by ~10%. 16 GPU pool is about 1.8x list of 8 pool but reduces tail risk and number of fallbacks. for pilots we often recommend starting 8 GPU + 40% burst and then shift to 16 if sustained peaks persist.
[05:06] Maya: any quick numbers for per-token cost delta when you switch to quantized fallback?
[05:09] Diego: roughly 30–45% cheaper per-token on quantized small variant but quality delta varies — depends on your prompts and embeddings.
[05:16] Ravi: operationally, if we go 8 GPU + 40% burst, what's our warm worker count during peaks?
[05:21] Diego: with 8 GPUs at base, burst buffer 40% equates to around 3 extra warm workers (depends on model size). effectively you're absorbing the first minute of ramp before autoscale completes.
[05:32] Noah: what about our region — we're in us-east-1, any provisioning slowness?
[05:36] Diego: Redwood has warm pools in us-east, but for Dedicated we provision customer pool in target region; initial cold provisioning can take longer, but burst buffer is the mitigation.
[05:44] Elena: for the on‑prem smoke test — what do you need from us?
[05:47] Jordan: staging access, kube creds (read-only for Redwood), and the traffic replay job. We'll coordinate dates.
[05:53] Priya: security checklist — SOC2 docs, KMS integration doc, and HSM requirements. we'll drop a short list in the shared drive.
[05:59] Samira: great. any blockers?
[06:02] Maya: none besides us gathering traffic traces; we'll prioritize that.
[06:07] Ravi: quick nit — the transcript we saw mentioned "K V cash" in transcription, haha.
[06:11] Diego: yeah fireflies sometimes does that.
[06:14] Samira: wrap up — recap action items (see chat), Diego run sims, Maya send traces, Samira update pricing, Jordan schedule smoke test, Priya send security checklist. we'll reconvene same time next week.
[06:28] Elena: can we also get a short doc that compares 8 vs 16 pool in perf numbers? 1 pager?
[06:32] Samira: yes Samira will produce a 1-pager with perf/cost tradeoffs and share with the team.
[06:36] Noah: anything else?
[06:38] Maya: no, thanks everyone.
[06:40] Samira: thanks, meeting end.
